p: The sky 'opens' when a prophet is about to see God's world.
b: The heavens opening is the stage setting for a vision. Stephen sees the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand (Acts 7:56), and the heavens open over Jesus at his baptism (Matthew 3:16). In Revelation heaven stands open for the rider on the white horse (Revelation 19:11). Here the opening comes in Babylon, far from the Temple, and what Ezekiel sees is a throne that moves.

p: A canal near Nippur in Babylonia, not a natural river.
b: The Hebrew word nahar is usually 'river', but in Babylonia it also means a canal cut from the Euphrates. A canal called the Kebar (Akkadian naru kabari) appears in business records of the fifth century BC from Nippur, in the archive of the Murashu family, who leased land to Judean and other tenants. That fits the book's setting: the exiles were put to work on the king's land, rebuilding the economy of the countryside. The site of Tel-abib is not known (see 3:15).

a: the word of the LORD came, truly came
t: The word of the LORD came, truly came
p: The LORD is YHWH; the verb is doubled for emphasis; the voice shifts to 'he'.
b: The LORD, in capitals, stands for the divine name YHWH, as in most English Bibles; "Adonai" is "the Lord" and "Adonai YHWH" is "the Lord GOD". The Hebrew here doubles the verb (hayo hayah, 'coming it came'), a way of saying 'it truly came'. This verse is also the one place at the start where the prophet's name is given in the third person: the name Ezekiel (Yechezqel, 'God strengthens' or 'may God strengthen') appears only here and in 24:24. Everything else in chapter 1 is 'I'. Some see a later hand in the verse; others, an editor's heading or the prophet's own change of voice for a formal statement.
orig: הָיֹה הָיָה דְבַר־יְהוָה (hayo hayah devar YHWH)

p: The people of southern Babylonia, whose dynasty ruled Babylon.
b: The Hebrew Kasdim is 'the Chaldeans': the people of southern Babylonia, whose dynasty under Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar ruled Babylon from 626 BC. Ezekiel and the other prophets use the word for the Babylonian empire, so 'the land of the Chaldeans' is Babylonia. Later, in Daniel, the word also names a class of learned men.

a: the hand of the LORD was on him
p: A phrase for being seized by God, from here to the last vision.
b: 'The hand of the LORD' marks the moments when Ezekiel is overpowered and taken into a vision or a sign. It returns at 3:14, 3:22, 8:1, 33:22, 37:1 and 40:1. Elsewhere in the prophets the hand falls on Elisha before he prophesies (2 Kings 3:15) and on Isaiah as a strong warning (Isaiah 8:11). It is not a gentle touch. Ezekiel sometimes feels it as a weight (3:14). In Codex Vaticanus (printed by Swete) the Greek reads "on me", in the first person, like the rest of the chapter; the Plain follows the Hebrew "on him" (see the variant at 1:3).
r: Ezekiel 3:14; Ezekiel 3:22; Ezekiel 8:1; Ezekiel 37:1; Ezekiel 40:1; 2 Kings 3:15; Isaiah 8:11

a: a storm wind coming from the north
p: God arrives in a storm, and enemies came from the north.
b: Storm and fire are the old signs of God's coming (Psalm 18:7-15; Nahum 1:3; Job 38:1). The north has two meanings here. It is the direction from which Babylon's armies struck Judah (Jeremiah 1:13-15; 4:6), and in older poetry it is the mountain of the gods, Zaphon (Psalm 48:2; Isaiah 14:13). Ezekiel's readers would sense both: the LORD comes with the force of their conquerors, and from the north, the place of the great king. Babylonian and Canaanite storm gods, such as Baal, also came in cloud and lightning, and the Bible borrows the image to say that only the LORD truly rides the storm.

p: A rare word, only in Ezekiel; 'glowing metal' is a guess from context.
b: The Hebrew chashmal occurs only in Ezekiel (here, 1:27 and 8:2). The Greek Old Testament renders it elektron, which can mean amber or an alloy of gold and silver, and the KJV followed with 'amber'. Most scholars think it means a gleaming metal, perhaps glowing hot. Modern Hebrew uses chashmal for 'electricity', a word taken from this verse in the 1800s; that is a modern borrowing, not a claim that Ezekiel saw electricity. Rabbinic tradition treated the word as a secret: see Hagigah 13a.

a: the likeness of four living creatures
p: The word demut, 'likeness', hedges almost every part of the vision.
b: Ezekiel does not say he saw four living creatures. He says he saw the likeness (demut) of four living creatures, and from now on he hedges almost every description with 'like' or 'the appearance of'. The chain grows longer as the vision rises, until it reaches 'the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD' (1:28). The Plain keeps the hedges. They are not weakness: they say that what he saw cannot be put into words and that he is describing, not photographing. The living creatures (chayyot) are called cherubim in chapter 10 (10:15, 20).

p: Probably legs without a bend, not like an animal's.
b: The Hebrew says 'their leg was one straight leg'. Most take it to mean legs that were straight, not bent at the knee like an animal's hind legs; some take it to mean a single column with no joint, which the calf's foot below then finishes. The wording is odd and leaves the shape open.

p: In 10:14 the ox face is called a cherub's face.
b: The four faces are a human, a lion, an ox (shor) and an eagle. In chapter 10, which tells the same vision again, the list is the same except that the face that should be the ox's is called 'the face of the cherub' (10:14). Some commentators think cherub was the older word and that the ox is how Ezekiel describes a cherub's face; others think the text of 10:14 was altered. Jewish tradition has its own answer: the Talmud says the ox's face was changed to a cherub's so that the ox, which recalls the golden calf, could not be used to accuse Israel (Babylonian Talmud, Hagigah 13b). In the church the four faces became the four Gospels, and the ox is Luke's symbol in both Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.11.8) and Jerome; they match the other three differently (see the book page). The creatures wear the faces of the strongest in each part of creation: wild beast, tame beast, bird, human.

a: Wherever the spirit was about to go
p: The Hebrew ruach means spirit, wind and breath.
b: The same word, ruach, means 'wind', 'breath' and 'spirit'. In 1:4 it is a 'storm wind'. Here it is the force that moves the creatures and the wheels; it may be God's Spirit, or the wind-like power in the cloud. The Plain says 'spirit' and flags it here. The word returns for the spirit that lifts and enters the prophet (2:2; 3:12, 14, 24) and in the wordplay of the dry bones (37:1-14). Greek pneuma, like the Hebrew, covers both wind and spirit.

a: One wheel was on the ground
p: The wheels are called ofannim here and galgal in chapter 10.
b: The wheels (ofannim) go with the living creatures wherever the spirit sends them. In 10:13 the wheels are called galgal, 'whirling' wheels, and the Plain notes the change there. The picture is of two wheels set at right angles, a wheel inside a wheel, so that the chariot can run in any of four directions without turning (1:17). They are full of eyes (1:18) and move because the spirit of the living creature is in them (1:20-21).

p: Why scholars do not read Ezekiel's wheels as a spacecraft.
b: In 1968 Erich von Däniken's Chariots of the Gods? argued that Ezekiel described a spaceship, and in 1974 Josef Blumrich, an engineer who had worked for NASA, wrote The Spaceships of Ezekiel and drew a machine from the details. These books were widely read. Biblical scholars reject the reading for the same reasons they give for any ancient text: the vision belongs to a prophet's call and is told with the hedges of a vision (see 1:5), the throne carries the LORD and not a crew, and the details fit the throne-chariot images of Babylonian, Egyptian and Canaanite art and of the Temple's cherub-carried ark (1 Chronicles 28:18). The idea is a modern one, and the answer to it is the text itself: Ezekiel says he saw the glory of the LORD.

p: A gleaming gem named for Tarshish, far in the west.
b: The Hebrew is 'the appearance of tarshish', a precious stone named for the distant port. Ancient and modern guesses include topaz, beryl and chrysolite (a yellow-green gem). It is also one of the stones in the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:20), and Ezekiel counts it among the king of Tyre's jewels (28:13, in another part). The Greek has Tharsis; the KJV 'beryl'.

p: The all-seeing eyes of the throne; compare Revelation.
b: Eyes in the rims show that the throne sees everywhere: 'the eyes of the LORD run to and fro through the whole earth' (Zechariah 4:10). In Revelation the four creatures are 'full of eyes in front and behind' (Revelation 4:6). The wheels in chapter 10 also have eyes (10:12).

a: the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels
p: The Hebrew says 'the living creature' in the singular.
b: The Hebrew has 'the spirit of the living creature' in the singular, and again at 1:22 ('over the heads of the living creature'). The four are felt as one being moving as one, and in 10:15, 20 the prophet says 'it was the living creature I saw by the Kebar canal.' The Plain keeps the singular where the Hebrew has it, which is why 1:22 reads 'the heads of the living creature' beside 'their heads'. In this verse Codex Vaticanus (Swete) has 'where the cloud was, the spirit was to go' and 'a spirit of life' in the wheels (see the variant).

p: Not the 'firmament' of the KJV.
b: Raqia' comes from a verb for beating metal flat, so it is something hammered out and spread. It is the word for the sky in Genesis 1:6-8. The KJV's 'firmament' came through the Latin firmamentum, which Jerome took from the Greek stereoma, 'a solid thing', and so gave the word a sense of a hard shell that the Hebrew does not necessarily state. The Plain uses 'dome', as a neutral picture. Here the dome is a floor under the throne, as in Exodus 24:10. The Hebrew says 'over the heads of the living creature', in the singular, as in 1:20 (see the note there); the Plain keeps the singular.

p: Qerach means ice, frost or crystal.
b: Qerach is ice or something that looks like it, such as rock crystal. The Greek has krystallos. The dome shines with a cold, clear light that makes people afraid, as the Hebrew says ('awesome'). Revelation sees a sea of glass 'like crystal' in front of the throne (Revelation 4:6).

a: like the voice of the Almighty
p: The KJV's 'voice of speech' is a likely mistranslation of 'tumult'.
b: The Hebrew says 'the sound of tumult (hamullah), like the sound of a camp'. The KJV has 'the voice of speech', which gives the word a sense it does not seem to carry elsewhere; most modern English versions say 'tumult' or 'roar'. 'The Almighty' is Shaddai, a very old name for God, used in the stories of the patriarchs and in Job. The sound of the wings is the sound of a flood, of God, and of an army getting under way.

p: The ancient 'sapphire' was probably lapis lazuli.
b: The Hebrew sappir is not the modern clear blue sapphire. It was probably lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone with flecks of gold that Mesopotamians prized. In Exodus 24:10 the elders saw God's feet standing on 'something like a pavement of sapphire-like stone'. Ezekiel puts the same blue under the throne.

a: a likeness that looked like a human
p: The figure on the throne has the 'likeness' of Genesis 1.
b: The throne rider has the likeness of an adam, a human being. The word 'likeness' (demut) is the one Genesis 1:26 uses for humans: 'in our likeness'. Some see a hint here that humans were made in the image of the God who has such a form; Daniel sees one 'like a son of man' coming to the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:13). The hedge is strong even here: it is a likeness of the likeness of a human.

a: the bow that is in the clouds
p: The rainbow of the flood story now frames God's throne.
b: Qeshet is the ordinary word for a bow; it is also the 'bow' God set in the cloud as a sign of his promise after the flood (Genesis 9:13-16). Ezekiel sees in the glory of a rainstorm sky both mercy and judgment, since the same rainbow encircles the throne in Revelation (Revelation 4:3). It is a sign that the God of this terrible vision is still the God of the covenant with Noah.

a: the likeness of the glory of the LORD
p: The last and longest hedge; kavod is the book's key word.
b: Kavod comes from a root meaning 'heavy', and so 'weight', 'importance', 'honor'. When it is used of the LORD it means his visible presence, shining and heavy with importance. The chain of hedges ('the appearance of the likeness of the glory') is the longest in the vision. This is the glory that leaves the Temple (10:4, 18-19; 11:22-23) and returns to the new one (43:1-5). Ezekiel's fall on his face is the usual response (3:23; 43:3; 44:4).

p: God's address to Ezekiel, about 93 times: a mortal, a human being.
b: Ben adam, 'son of man', is God's way of speaking to Ezekiel, 93 times in the book. In Hebrew it simply means a human being, a mortal, as in Psalm 8:4. Set beside the glory of chapter 1 it reminds him how small he is. Rashi gives two reasons: that Ezekiel, who had seen the Chariot and moved among angels, is told that he is only a human being, and that the title keeps him from becoming proud of his closeness to the Chariot (reported from Sefaria). The Greek is huios anthropou. Whether the title carries a larger sense is debated; the Gospel title 'the Son of Man' is a different question, taken up in the topic page.

p: Ruach again: what stands the prophet up.
b: The spirit enters Ezekiel and sets him on his feet; the same thing happens at 3:24. At 3:12 and 3:14 a spirit lifts him, and at 8:3 and 11:1 the spirit lifts him again to be taken in vision. The Hebrew ruach is the same word as the wind of 1:4, and some readers think the 'spirit' is the Spirit of the LORD (11:5 says so). Christian readers often hear the Holy Spirit; the Plain keeps the plain word.

p: The Hebrew says 'nations'; the Greek has only 'house of Israel'.
b: The Hebrew says 'to the Israelites, to nations of rebels'. Calling Israel 'nations' (goyim) is strange, since Israel is usually the one people set against the nations. Some think it points to the two kingdoms, Israel and Judah, or uses 'nation' as an insult (compare Isaiah 1:4). The Greek in Swete's text has only 'the house of Israel, those who embitter me'. The Plain follows the Hebrew; see the variant.

p: A messenger's opening words; 'Lord GOD' is Adonai YHWH.
b: Koh amar Adonai YHWH, 'thus says the Lord GOD', is the formula of a messenger delivering a king's words. Ezekiel uses 'Adonai YHWH' (the Lord GOD) 217 times; the book's constant use of it stresses that God is master even of the exile. In the Hebrew the second word is the divine name, which Jewish readers did not pronounce and read as 'Adonai'; to avoid 'Lord LORD', the usual English printing is 'Lord GOD'. The prophet adds nothing: 'The Lord GOD says this' stands alone, to be said to a people who may refuse to hear it.
orig: כֹּה אָמַר אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה (koh amar Adonai YHWH)

p: Beit meri: Ezekiel's name for his hearers.
b: Beit meri, 'rebellious house', is one of Ezekiel's names for Israel (2:5, 6, 7, 8; 3:9, 26, 27; 12:2-3, 9, 25; 17:12; 24:3; 44:6). Meri means rebellion against a master. The Plain gives one English phrase each time. Note the end of the verse: even rebels will know that 'a prophet has been among them', whether they listen or not. The aim is not that they obey but that they cannot say no one warned them.

p: Two rare words for prickly plants, then scorpions.
b: The two words sarabim and sallonim are rare, and no one is sure which plants they name; 'thistles and thorns' gives the general idea. Scorpions are real desert creatures that sting, and the picture is of the prophet's hearers as a dangerous place to live. The line is a parallel to the 'hard faces' of 2:4 and 3:8-9.

p: The scroll holds funeral words.
b: The words are qinim (laments, the funeral songs of Lamentations and Ezekiel 19), hegeh (a low moan, sighing) and hi (woe, found nowhere else). The scroll written on front and back is crowded, like the stone tablets of Exodus 32:15 and the scroll in Revelation 5:1, so that nothing can be added. What the prophet will bring is not a hope but a long dirge, and the scroll turns sweet in the mouth (3:3) because it is God's word, not because it is pleasant.

p: Eating God's words; compare Jeremiah and Revelation.
b: To eat the scroll is to take God's words in completely before speaking them. Jeremiah says almost the same of his own call (Jeremiah 15:16). The psalmists find God's words sweeter than honey (Psalm 19:10; 119:103). In Revelation 10:9-10 the little scroll is sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach; Ezekiel's own bitterness comes at 3:14. Ellen Davis (Swallowing the Scroll) argues that the scene marks the move from speech to writing in prophecy.

p: A foreign, hard-to-follow language.
b: The Hebrew is 'deep of lip and heavy of tongue': speech too deep to follow. The same idea shows in Isaiah 33:19 ('a people of obscure speech') and in Moses' complaint that he was 'heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue' (Exodus 4:10). The point is a bitter one: foreigners with a language Ezekiel could not understand would have listened if he had been sent to them; his own people, who speak his language, will not.

a: they would have listened to you
p: Jesus says the same of Tyre, Sidon and Sodom.
b: The claim that outsiders would have listened is echoed in the story of Jonah, where the Ninevites repent at once, and in Jesus' words that Tyre, Sidon and Sodom would have repented at his miracles (Matthew 11:21-24). In each place it is a charge against those who have had every advantage.

p: A very hard stone or point, used for carving.
b: Shamir names a very hard material. Jeremiah says Judah's sin is written 'with a point of shamir' (Jeremiah 17:1), and Zechariah speaks of hearts made like shamir (Zechariah 7:12). It could be emery (a hard natural abrasive), corundum or flint; the word 'diamond' is a traditional guess. Ezekiel's forehead will be harder than flint, so that it can face the hard foreheads of the house of Israel (3:7).

a: Blessed be the glory of the LORD from its place!
p: A famous line in Jewish prayer; some propose a one-letter change.
b: These words are the Kedushah, the response said in the daily synagogue prayers. The Hebrew barukh, 'blessed', fits what the angels say, and Codex Vaticanus (Swete) reads 'blessed' like the Hebrew. Because a spirit has just 'lifted' the prophet, some commentators propose changing one letter to read berum, 'as it rose up', so that the glory itself rises from its place; this is a conjecture, not a reading found in a witness. The 'rumbling' of the wheels and wings is the same sound as in 1:24.

a: I went away bitter, with my spirit boiling
p: Why Ezekiel is angry is not said.
b: Marah, 'bitter', and chemah, 'heat, rage', describe the prophet's mood after the sweetness of the scroll. The text does not say whom he is angry with: the people, God for sending him, or himself. Jeremiah's cries against his call are the nearest parallel (Jeremiah 15:17-18; 20:7-9). The 'hand of the LORD' is strong on him (compare 1:3).

p: Not 'Spring Hill' in Hebrew: a Babylonian ruin mound.
b: Tel is a mound built up from the ruins of a town, so Tel-abib is a mound village. The second part may come from the Akkadian til abubi, 'mound of the flood', an old ruined town left by a flood, which the Hebrew heard as aviv, 'spring' or 'new grain'. In 1902 Nahum Sokolow used 'Tel Aviv' to translate the title of Herzl's novel Altneuland, and the new city on the coast took the name from this verse, though the biblical village was in Babylonia. The site of Ezekiel's Tel-abib is not known.

p: Shamam: stunned, shattered, mourning in silence.
b: Mashmim comes from shamem, 'to be desolate or appalled'. Ezekiel sits stunned for seven days, the length of the mourning period (Genesis 50:10; Job 2:13, where Job's friends sit seven days in silence). He mourns the Temple and the city before he speaks.

a: a watchman for the house of Israel
p: A sentry on the wall who must warn of the enemy.
b: A tsofeh stood on a city wall and blew a horn if an army came (33:2-6). The prophet is that watchman. Other prophets use the picture (Isaiah 21:6-12; 56:10; Jeremiah 6:17; Habakkuk 2:1; Hosea 9:8). The duty is to speak, and the outcome is not in his hands: he saves his own life by warning, whether or not they listen (3:19, 21). Paul uses similar words when he says he is innocent of the blood of all (Acts 20:26-27). Chapter 33 comes back to the watchman (in another part of this book).

p: 'Avon is guilt; chatta't is sin.
b: The Plain keeps 'avon as 'guilt' (also the debt and punishment that follow wrongdoing) and chatta't as 'sin'. To 'bear the guilt' is the regular Hebrew phrase for answering for it (4:4-6). The wicked person dies for his own guilt, not for the prophet's; the prophet is answerable only if he stays silent.

a: I will demand his blood from your hand
p: A murder charge laid on a silent watchman.
b: 'I will demand blood from the hand of' is the language of a murder trial (Genesis 9:5; 42:22; 2 Samuel 4:11). The silent watchman is treated like a killer, because he could have saved a life. Chapters 3 and 33 are the two places where Ezekiel is told this; chapter 18 then says that each person answers for his own life.

a: I put a stumbling block in front of him
p: A hard line: how the same God warns and trips.
b: That the LORD sets a stumbling block before a righteous person who turns away is hard to square with his warning. Readers take it as a test that exposes the heart (Jeremiah 6:21), as judgment on a person who is already turning, or as a way of saying that falling is the outcome of turning away. Jewish and Christian teachers (and Calvinists and Arminians) have read it in line with their views of freedom and grace. The verse should be read with 14:3-4, 7 and chapter 18.

a: the glory of the LORD was standing
t: The glory stands on the plain
p: The same glory as at the canal, now in the plain.
b: The glory seen in chapter 1 comes to Ezekiel again, 'like the glory I had seen by the Kebar canal', in a valley plain (biq'ah). The word returns in 37:1, where he stands in a plain full of bones. The glory then appears in the Temple (8:4), leaves (10:4, 18-19; 11:22-23) and comes back (43:1-5).

a: they will put ropes on you
p: Who ties him is not said; at 4:8 God does.
b: The Hebrew has 'they will put ropes on you', and it is not said who they are. In 4:8 the LORD himself puts ropes on Ezekiel so that he cannot turn from one side to the other. Some read the ropes as the prophet's neighbors binding a man they thought mad; others read them as the LORD's way of holding him to his task.

p: A silence broken only by God, and ended in 33:22.
b: The muteness runs from here to 33:22, when a survivor from Jerusalem brings the news of the fall. What it means is debated. It may be total silence, except when God gave him a message (3:27; 24:27); Moshe Greenberg's study of it in 1958 is the starting point for the view that it limited his role, since the Hebrew says he will not be a 'man who reproves' (ish mokhiach), a word that can also mean an arbiter or intercessor. Some think he went silent for only some of the time. Old psychiatric diagnoses (catalepsy, paralysis) belong to a modern tradition and have critics who note that the text presents the silence as God's act.

t: A clay brick as a map
p: Babylonian scribes drew plans on clay.
b: A brick of soft clay was the exiles' notebook. Babylonian scribes drew plans of cities and fields on clay tablets, and the plan of the city of Nippur (about 1500 BC) is the best known. Ezekiel is told to scratch Jerusalem on a brick and build a toy siege around it, a plan that his neighbors in Babylonia would have recognized.

a: This is a sign for the house of Israel.
p: Whether Ezekiel really did these acts.
b: A sign (ot) is a message acted out. Other prophets did the same (Isaiah 20:2-4; Jeremiah 13:1-11; 19:1-13; Hosea 1:2-9). Some scholars, including Zimmerli and Block, take Ezekiel's acts as performed in public. Others think some were visions or literary scenes that were never physically carried out. The text itself gives no sign that they are not real. The iron plate (4:3) is the wall between the LORD and the city, not just a pan.

a: lay the guilt of the house of Israel on it
p: Ezekiel carries the people's guilt, as priests did.
b: To 'bear' (nasa') guilt ('avon) means to carry its weight and its penalty. Priests were said to bear the people's guilt (Leviticus 10:17), and the goat on the Day of Atonement carried it away (Leviticus 16:21-22). Ezekiel is a priest. Whether he is carrying it in the sense of paying for it or only showing it is debated. The 'it' is ambiguous: the Hebrew says 'on it', which could mean on the side he lies on, or on him.

a: I have set for you the years
t: Do the days fit the dates?
p: A count: 7 + 390 + 40 = 437 days, set beside the dates in 1:2 and 8:1.
b: The first vision is dated the fifth day of the fourth month of the fifth year (1:1-2), and the next date in the book is the fifth day of the sixth month of the sixth year (8:1). That is 14 months, about 413 days with months of 29 and 30 days. The seven days at Tel-abib (3:15), the 390 days on the left side and the 40 on the right (4:5-6) add up to 437, more than 413 if all of them ran one after another before 8:1. A leap month changes the count. The calendar added a thirteenth month in some years to keep the months in step with the seasons, and one such month inside the window would make it about 443 days, which holds 437 with room to spare. Two more things stay open. The text does not say that the 390 and 40 days were finished by 8:1, only that on that date Ezekiel is sitting in his house with the elders. It also does not say that he lay on his side through the whole of each day. The Greek's 190 days (see the variant) would fit easily either way. So the arithmetic does not settle whether, or how, the acts were carried out as written.

a: wheat, barley, broad beans, lentils, millet and spelt
p: Six grains and pulses mixed in one jar: the bread of a siege.
b: The list is a poor person's pantry: grains and pulses mixed because no single one is left. Twenty shekels of it a day is about 230 grams (8 ounces), and a sixth of a hin of water is about 0.6 liter (a little over a pint). It is the rationing that Leviticus 26:26 describes, 'bread by weight'. Ezekiel eats siege rations while he lies on his side.

p: Unclean fuel, and a word that sounds like 'filthy idols'.
b: The Hebrew gelele tse'at ha'adam uses gelel, 'dung pellets', the root that gives gillulim, 'filthy idols', in 6:4. The law in Deuteronomy 23:12-14 tells Israel to bury human waste outside the camp so that the camp stays holy, and this meal would make Ezekiel, a priest, unclean in plain view (4:14). Cow dung, a common fuel in the Near East, is the permitted substitute (4:15).

p: Exile means eating unclean food.
b: For a people with food laws, exile among the nations meant unclean food. Hosea says the same of Ephraim in Assyria (Hosea 9:3-4), and Daniel refuses the king's food for this reason (Daniel 1:8). The sign makes concrete what the exile will be like for those still in Jerusalem.

a: I myself have not been made unclean
p: Peter says almost the same in Acts 10:14.
b: Ezekiel objects as a priest. He has kept the rules that priests keep: no animal found dead and none torn by beasts (Leviticus 22:8; Ezekiel 44:31). In Acts 10:14 Peter answers a heavenly command to eat with very similar words. In both stories the command is changed, here by a lesser uncleanness, in Acts by God's cleansing.

p: A technical word for sacrificial meat eaten too late.
b: Pigul in the law means meat from an offering that is eaten after its allowed time, and it makes the offering unacceptable (Leviticus 7:18; 19:7). The KJV's 'abominable flesh' is a loose rendering. Isaiah 65:4 uses a related word for a broth of such meat. The Greek here has a word for 'stale' meat. Ezekiel says he has never eaten any kind of ritually spoiled food.

p: Bread is the staff a person leans on.
b: 'Staff of bread' is the picture of bread as the stick a person leans on; when it breaks, he falls. The phrase is from Leviticus 26:26, where the LORD threatens it, and returns in 5:16 and 14:13. Psalm 105:16 says the LORD called down a famine and broke every staff of bread.

a: the kind a barber uses as a razor
p: Isaiah calls Assyria a hired razor.
b: Shaving the head and beard was a shame and a sign of mourning (Isaiah 7:20, where the LORD shaves Judah with a razor hired beyond the River; Isaiah 15:2). A priest was not to shave his head (Ezekiel 44:20). Ezekiel uses a sword for a razor: the Babylonian sword is God's razor on Jerusalem.

a: Burn a third of it in the fire in the middle of the city
p: Fire, sword and wind: the three fates, with a fourth in the hem.
b: A third burned in the city (famine and plague, as in 5:12), a third struck by the sword around the city, a third scattered to the wind: the three ends of the people. A few are saved in the hem of the robe, and even some of those are thrown into the fire (5:3-4). Zechariah 13:8-9 has a similar one-third left, to be refined.

a: From it a fire will go out
p: Who are the survivors in the hem?
b: Even the few saved in the hem of his robe are partly burned. Readers see the small group that survives the fall of Jerusalem and then suffers again, as in the killing of Gedaliah and the flight to Egypt (Jeremiah 41-44). The fire that goes out 'to the whole house of Israel' means that even the exiles will not be safe from what began in the city.

a: in the middle of the nations
p: Ezekiel's 'center' is a place of responsibility, not only honor.
b: Later Jewish writing made Jerusalem the 'navel of the earth': Jubilees 8:19 puts Zion at the world's center, and 1 Enoch 26:1 calls the place 'the middle of the earth'. Ezekiel 38:12 uses 'navel of the earth' of Israel. Here the point is a heavy one: because she has the LORD's laws before the eyes of all the nations, Jerusalem's failure is worse (5:6).

p: Mishpatim and chuqqot: the site always renders them the same.
b: Mishpatim are 'rulings', God's decisions of what is right in particular cases; chuqqot are 'rules', fixed laws. The two are Ezekiel's way of saying the whole Torah (compare 18:5-9; 20:11-25). The KJV and many translations say 'judgments' and 'statutes'. In 5:7 they become the center of a charge: they broke God's laws and even fell below the nations'.

a: Your uproar is greater than that of the nations
p: Hamon: tumult. The last clause says 'not even'; 11:12 says the opposite.
b: Hamon means a crowd, a roar, a tumult: Jerusalem is louder and more restless than the nations around her. The same word can also mean 'multitude' or 'abundance', which would give 'you have outdone the nations'; the Plain takes the sense of tumult. The last clause says that they have not even acted by the rulings of the nations around them; in 11:12 the opposite is said, that they have acted by the nations' rulings. Codex Vaticanus (Swete) has the same negative as the Hebrew here, but the apparatus of the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia reports Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac without the 'not', which would bring the verse into line with 11:12 (see the variant). If the 'not' is original, readers explain the clash as two charges (they broke the LORD's laws and did not even reach the nations' standards), as a difference of audience, or as a slip; if it was dropped, the clash disappears, though a scribe may also have removed the 'not' to make the two verses agree.

a: fathers will eat their sons in your midst
p: A curse of the covenant, and what happened in the siege.
b: Eating one's children is the worst of the covenant curses (Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53-57). It happened in the siege of Samaria (2 Kings 6:28-29), and Jeremiah and Lamentations speak of it in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 19:9; Lamentations 2:20; 4:10). Ezekiel is the only one to add that sons will also eat fathers.

p: Ne'um: an 'utterance'.
b: Ne'um is a noun, 'an utterance of the LORD', placed beside the name of the speaker, as in 'the Lord GOD declares'. In Hebrew it often comes at the end or in the middle of a sentence to make the words a formal pronouncement. The oath 'as I live' that goes with it is the strongest oath God swears.

p: Shiqqutsim, to'evot and gillulim are different words.
b: Ezekiel names three words for idol worship and what goes with it. Shiqqutsim are 'detestable things', things that disgust (7:20; 11:18, 21); to'evot are 'abhorrent things', practices that the LORD abhors (5:9, 11; 6:9, 11; 7:3-4, 8-9); and gillulim are 'filthy idols', a mocking word. The Plain keeps the three apart. Here two of them stand together, because the sanctuary was made unclean by both.

a: I myself will shave you down
p: 'Egra' may be a pun on the razor of 5:1.
b: The verb gara' means 'to trim, reduce, take away'. Here it is probably a pun on the razor of 5:1: God himself will shave the people. Others read 'withdraw' (my favor, or my eye), as the Greek does ('I will thrust you away'). The Qumran scroll 11QEzek has the word only in a restored form, so it gives no help.

p: One English word for dever in Ezekiel: plague.
b: The Hebrew dever is a deadly outbreak, often joined with sword and famine (5:12, 17; 6:11-12; 7:15; 12:16; 14:19, 21; 33:27; 38:22). This Plain English renders it "plague" every time in Ezekiel, as in Leviticus 26:25. Jeremiah's Plain uses "disease" for the same word, and each book keeps its own choice throughout. In Ezekiel's lists "sword, famine, wild animals and plague" are the four terrible judgments of 14:21.

a: let my rage rest on them
p: The Plain gives each Hebrew word for God's anger one English word.
b: Ezekiel uses several words for God's anger, and the Plain keeps them apart as Lamentations does. Af is "anger" (the nose that snorts); chemah, from the verb "to be hot", is "rage" (5:13, 15; 6:12; 7:8; 13:13; 16:38; 20:8 and many more); 'evrah, an overflow, is "fury" (7:19; 21:31; 22:21, 31; 38:19); za'am is "indignation" (21:31; 22:24, 31). So in the phrase "my anger will be spent, and I will let my rage rest" two different words are in play. "Rage rest" or "rage settle" (5:13; 16:42; 21:17; 24:13) is a set expression for God's anger being satisfied.

a: Then they will know that I, the LORD, have spoken in my jealousy
t: Then they will know that I am the LORD
p: The refrain of the book, in its two main forms.
b: This is the first form of Ezekiel's refrain: 'that I, the LORD, have spoken'. The main form is 'Then they will know that I am the LORD' (6:7, 10, 13, 14; 7:4, 27). Counted in the Hebrew, a form of 'know' is followed directly by 'that I am the LORD' in 56 verses, and by 'that I am the Lord GOD' in five more (13:9; 23:49; 24:24; 28:24; 29:16): 61 in all. In some of them the Plain reads 'that I, the LORD, have spoken' or names another act of God after the verb (5:13; 17:21; 20:12; 21:5; 22:22; 34:30; 35:12; 36:36; 37:14). Other verses have 'I the LORD have spoken' without 'know' (5:15, 17; 21:17, 32; 22:14; 24:14; 26:14; 30:12; 34:24). The formula, which Walther Zimmerli named the 'recognition formula' (Erweiswort), ends both threats and promises: judgment and rescue alike make the LORD known. The Plain always writes it the same way. 'I will feel relief' is nicham, to be eased, as in Isaiah 1:24.
r: Ezekiel 6:7; Ezekiel 7:4; Ezekiel 36:11; Ezekiel 39:28; Isaiah 1:24; Exodus 6:7

p: Deuteronomy 32 has the same picture.
b: Famine, disease and beasts are arrows of God in the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:23-24). Ezekiel uses it for the siege, joined to the broken staff of bread of Leviticus 26:26.

p: Chapters 4-7 follow the covenant curses.
b: The wild animals that bereave (Leviticus 26:22), the sword and plague (26:25), the staff of bread (26:26), eating sons (26:29), the high places cut down and corpses on idols (26:30) and the scattering (26:33) all stand in Leviticus 26, in nearly the same order as in Ezekiel 4-6. Ezekiel's priestly eye reads the siege as the curses of the covenant coming due. Four judgments (sword, famine, wild animals, plague) are brought together in 14:21 (another part).

p: The mountains hold the shrines.
b: The mountains are addressed because they hold the shrines. Deuteronomy 12:2 tells Israel to destroy the places on high mountains and hills where nations served their gods. Ezekiel preaches to the land itself (36:1-15 says the same in hope).

p: Local altars on hills, which the Torah and the kings tried to end.
b: Bamot, 'high places', were local altars and shrines on hills. The Torah ordered them destroyed (Leviticus 26:30; Deuteronomy 12:2-3), and Josiah did so in 622 BC (2 Kings 23:8-20). Ezekiel says the work was not finished, since the people still came to them. The word has a pun in 20:29 (in another part).

p: Chammanim: a rare word for cult stands.
b: The word chammanim is rare; Leviticus 26:30, 2 Chronicles 34:4 and Isaiah 17:8 use it. Some think the root is chammah, 'sun', and read 'sun-pillars'; the Greek calls them 'shrines' (temene). The Plain's 'incense stands' matches this site's wording of Leviticus 26:30.

p: A mocking word that sounds like 'dung pellets'.
b: Gillulim is Ezekiel's special word for idols, found about 39 times. It looks like a word for 'dung pellets' (gelel; see 4:12), and probably also plays on galal, 'to roll'. It is a word of contempt, as if the gods were lumps of dung. The Greek uses eidola, 'idols'. 1 Kings 15:12 uses it too, and the Plain gives 'filthy idols' there. Leviticus 26:30, the verse Ezekiel is echoing, has the same word, which this site's Leviticus renders simply 'idols'; Ezekiel's 'filthy' is added to carry the contempt in the word. It is not the same as shiqqutsim (see 5:11).

p: Ye'shamu can mean 'be desolate' or 'be held guilty'.
b: The verb ye'shamu is from asham, usually 'be guilty'. Here it is paired with 'ruined' and the high places 'desolate', so some read it as 'be made desolate', from a second root. The Plain's 'bear the blame' keeps the sense of guilt. The altars are treated like people who must answer for what was done on them.

a: I will leave some of you alive
p: Not all die; survivors remember.
b: The theme of those who survive after judgment is a strong one in the prophets (Isaiah 10:20-22; Amos 9:8-10). In Ezekiel the survivors scattered among the nations are the ones who will remember the LORD (6:9), a first step toward the hope in later chapters. The Hebrew word here is pelitim, 'those who escaped'.

t: Heart and eyes that prostitute themselves
p: Numbers 15:39 uses the same two organs.
b: The pair 'heart' and 'eyes' that 'prostitute themselves' recalls Numbers 15:39, where tassels remind Israel not to follow its heart and eyes in prostitution. The picture of idolatry as prostitution runs through Hosea 1-3, Jeremiah 2-3 and Ezekiel 16 and 23. God says he was 'broken' by it: the injured husband.

a: Strike your hands together, stamp your foot
p: A gesture of horror, not of joy.
b: Clapping and stamping can show glee, as in 25:6 where Ammon does it over Jerusalem. Here the prophet does it as a dramatic sign of grief and horror at Israel's coming fate. Compare Numbers 24:10 for striking the hands.

p: Hanatsur can mean 'besieged' or 'guarded'.
b: Hanatsur is from tsur ('besiege') or natsar ('guard'). The first suits the context, since the siege-famine follows plague far away and sword nearby; the second would mean 'the one kept safe will die of famine'. Both readings end in death: no corner is safe.

p: The aroma that pleases the LORD is given to idols.
b: 'A soothing aroma' (re'ach nichoach) is the phrase for an offering the LORD accepts (Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9). Ezekiel says the people gave it to idols under every green tree and leafy terebinth, the old places of the Canaanite shrines (Deuteronomy 12:2; 2 Kings 17:10; Jeremiah 2:20).

p: A span from the wilderness to Diblah, or "more desolate than"; and a possible Riblah.
b: The Hebrew mimmidbar Diblatah can be read two ways. 'More desolate than the wilderness toward Diblah' takes the min as a comparison (the KJV and some other versions); 'from the wilderness to Diblah' takes it as a span, the whole land from south to north. The Plain follows the span, because the Greek reads it so ('from the wilderness Deblatha' in Swete's text) and because the phrase 'in all the places where they live' wants a whole country, not a comparison. Diblah is not known as a place elsewhere. Many commentators therefore think the original was Riblah, in the far north of Syria on the road to Babylon (the place where Nebuchadnezzar later judged Zedekiah, 2 Kings 25:6-7). The reason for the guess is that resh (r) and daleth (d) look almost the same in Hebrew writing, and that Riblah, not Diblah, makes sense as the northern end of a span that begins in the southern wilderness. It stays a conjecture: the Hebrew text and the Greek both read D.

a: An end! The end has come
p: A sound-play: qets ba haqets.
b: The Hebrew is qets ba haqets, a drumbeat of one word repeated. Amos used the same sound in a pun about a basket of summer fruit, qayits, and the end, qets (Amos 8:2), and Genesis 6:13 uses 'end' in the flood. The four corners (literally 'wings') are the four edges of the land. The Hebrew says 'the soil of Israel' (admat yisra'el), a phrase Ezekiel prefers to the usual word for land.

p: The Hebrew 'one disaster' is obscure.
b: The Hebrew ra'ah achat means 'a disaster, one': perhaps a disaster without parallel or one disaster following another. The KJV has 'an evil, an only evil'. The Plain keeps 'single' to leave both senses.

p: A second pun: qets, 'end', and heqitz, 'woke'.
b: The verb heqitz is from yaqats, 'wake'. It sounds like qets, 'end', so the end 'woke up' against Jerusalem. English cannot carry the pun, but the line shows the same relentless sound as 7:2.

p: A rare word: doom, turn, or cycle.
b: Tsefirah is rare and its meaning uncertain. In Isaiah 28:5 it means a wreath or crown; here it may mean a 'turn' of events, a cycle, or 'doom'. The Vulgate has a word for 'crushing' (contritio), and Swete's Greek puts 'the end' here, as in the verses around it. The next lines add 'panic' (mehumah) and a shout (hed) that does not come: the mountains, which echo with festival, will give no joy.

p: Aaron's rod flowers; this rod flowers with pride.
b: Matteh is a rod or staff. In Numbers 17:8 Aaron's rod blossoms as a sign of God's choice, and in Jeremiah 1:11 an almond branch (shaqed) wakes. Here the rod blossoms into arrogance. Readers differ on what it is: Nebuchadnezzar, the rod of God's punishment as in Isaiah 10:5; or Judah's own pride (Zedekiah), or violence in the land (7:11).

p: Several rare words; every version differs.
b: This verse has three nearly unknown words, hamehem, noah and perhaps hamon. Versions disagree: the KJV has 'neither shall there be wailing for them'; the BSB, 'none of their wealth, and nothing of value'; the Greek has 'he will break the support of the lawless'. The Plain gives the sense most common in modern translations and says so here.

a: The seller will never get back what he sold
p: A seller normally got his land back at the Jubilee.
b: Leviticus 25:13-28 says land that is sold goes back to its family in the Jubilee year. Ezekiel says the seller will not return: the exile will cancel the Jubilee, and there will be no return to ancestral land. The day of the LORD is not a Jubilee. The same thought shows in 7:12, where the buyer should not rejoice and the seller should not mourn: all the transactions are meaningless.

p: The word for the uncleanness of a woman's period.
b: Niddah is the uncleanness of a woman's monthly period (Leviticus 15:19-24). The Plain says 'an unclean thing' for the word here, as in Leviticus 20:21 and Lamentations 1:8, 17, where Jerusalem herself has become one. Silver and gold thrown in the street turn to filth. The same image that was a treasure is now to be avoided.

a: will not be able to save them
p: Zephaniah says the same.
b: The same claim, that silver and gold cannot save on the day of the LORD's wrath, is made in Zephaniah 1:18, and Proverbs 11:4 says wealth is of no use on the day of wrath. Ezekiel has just said that silver will be thrown away in the streets.

p: The Hebrew is 'his ornament': jewelry or the Temple?
b: The verse says 'the beauty of his ornament he set for pride'. The 'he' is not named. Some think it is the LORD, and the ornament is the Temple (Ezekiel 24:21 calls the sanctuary the pride of Judah's power); others that it is Israel and the ornament is the jewelry the LORD gave her, which she made into idols (16:11-17). The KJV says 'he set it in majesty'. The Plain passes over the 'he' by using a passive.

p: Tsefuni: the Holy of Holies, or what the LORD treasures.
b: Tsefuni is from tsafan, 'hide, store up'. So it can mean 'my hidden place' (the Holy of Holies, never seen by the people) or 'my treasured place'. The KJV and WEB have 'secret place'; the BSB 'treasured place'. In Psalm 83:3 the related word names those the LORD treasures. The Greek has 'my watching' or 'oversight' (episkope).

p: A rare word, perhaps for the chains of captivity.
b: Ratoq, 'chain', occurs only here in the singular. The plural is in 1 Kings 6:21 (gold chains) and Isaiah 40:19, and a verb from the same root is in Nahum 3:10, where the nobles are bound in chains. The call means: prepare chains for the captives, for the land is full of crimes and violence.

p: Mishpat damim: bloodshed, or sentences for bloodshed.
b: The phrase may mean unjust sentences that spill blood, or crimes of bloodshed that call for judgment. Both fit with 'violence' in the next line. The same pair of 'blood' and 'violence' is in 7:11 and 8:17.

p: An idiom for the most violent of the nations.
b: The Hebrew ra'ei goyim means 'the evil ones of the nations': the worst, most savage people. Babylonian armies are meant, though the text does not name them.

a: teaching will be lost from the priest
p: Torah as instruction; see Jeremiah 18:18.
b: The Hebrew torah here means instruction: the teaching the priest gave. The three channels of guidance, vision from the prophet, teaching from the priest and counsel from the elders, will all fail. Jeremiah 18:18 lists the same three as the voices the people trust; Micah 3:6 and Lamentations 2:9 speak of the prophets losing their vision.

a: the leader will be dressed in horror
p: The Plain says 'leader' for nasi', where the KJV says 'prince'.
b: Nasi' is 'leader', literally 'one lifted up' or chosen. The KJV and many versions say 'prince'. Ezekiel prefers nasi' to 'king' for the rulers of Judah (12:10, 12; 19:1; 21:25; 22:6) and for the future ruler of 40-48. The line puts 'king' and 'leader' side by side, so they may be two figures (Zedekiah and a high official) or one person described twice.

p: 'Am ha'arets: who is meant changes by passage.
b: 'Am ha'arets, 'the people of the land', is one phrase with different meanings in different places: landowners with political weight in Judah (2 Kings 21:24; 23:30), the poor farmers, or the people in general. The Plain gives one English phrase and a note wherever it matters. Ezekiel uses it also in 12:19; 22:29; 33:2; 39:13; 45:16, 22; 46:3, 9.

a: by their own judgments I will judge them
p: The measure they used is used on them.
b: The phrase 'by their judgments' means by the standards they set for others. The idea is measure for measure, as in Jesus' words about the measure you give (Matthew 7:2).
